subtype_info: Invasive aspergillosis of a pulmonary hydatid cyst
title: Invasive aspergillosis of pulmonary hydatid cyst
case_text:
A 50-year-old male diabetic was diagnosed and treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 13 years ago. He presented with a 6-month history of low-grade fever and sweating. He also had frequent hemoptysis for the previous 3 months. He was investigated at his local hospital and referred to us for management of pulmonary aspergiloma. Examination was significant for low-grade fever and bronchial breath sounds with coarse crepitations in the right infrascapular region. A sputum smear was negative for acid-fast bacilli and grew Aspergillus. A plain chest x-ray showed a thick wall cavity in the upper and mid zone adjacent to the right hilum. A high-resolution CT scan revealed a large cavity in the apical segment of the right lower lobe with extensive lamellar internal echoes (Figure 1). Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed a simple hepatic cyst with no internal echoes. Bronchoscopy showed fresh blood and some necrotic material coming out of the superior segment of the right lower lobe. Culture of the material grew Aspergillus.
Wedge resection of the apical segment of the right lower lobe was performed due to persistent hemoptysis and growth of Aspergillus species in a possible post tuberculous cavity. Gross examination of the specimen revealed a surprisingly whitish membrane of the cyst wall with fungal necrotic material inside (Figure 2). Histopathological examination confirmed the presence of hydatid cyst along with echinoccocus hooklets with invasive Aspergillus within the cyst wall (Figure 2). Lung tissue around the cyst showed nonspecific chronic inflammation and an absence of fungal hyphae. The patient was treated for hydatid disease with albendazole and itraconazole for aspergillosis. The patient was free of any recurrence of either disease at the 8-month follow-up.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Invasive aspergillosis of a pulmonary hydatid cyst
